transcript.content: Hello, welcome to the clinic. Can you tell me what brings you in today?

Hi, yeah, thanks for seeing me. So, what brings me in... well, it's mostly my work. I'm an electrician, been doing it for years, and I've always been careful, you know? You have to be in my line of work, or things go wrong, houses burn down. But lately... well, for a while now, honestly, I just keep going back over my jobs again and again. 

Like, I'll finish up a panel, a really simple install that I've done a thousand times, but then I'm standing there checking the breakers. Over and over. And the labels, I have to make sure every single label is exactly right, perfectly lined up. I even check the torque marks on the lugs to make absolutely sure they're tightened down, even though I know I just did it. I've even started taking photos on my phone before I close up a box, just so I can look at them later to reassure myself. But half the time that doesn't even help, because I'll be driving home, like halfway down the highway, and I just get this nagging feeling and I actually turn my truck around and drive all the way back to the site just to look at the panel one more time in person. 

It’s getting to the point where a basic install is taking me way, way longer than it should. Hours longer, sometimes. And people are starting to notice. The general contractors, the other guys on the crew... they're making comments, looking at me weird, asking what's taking so long in the utility room, and I just... I can't seem to just pack up my tools and leave like a normal person anymore.
When you're checking your work over and over, are you having thoughts that come into your mind that you don’t want there—like a fear that something bad will happen if everything isn’t perfect?

Yeah. Yeah, exactly. It’s exactly like that. It’s like... I know I checked it. I know I did. I can literally see myself doing it in my memory, but then this... this thought just barges right in anyway. It’s always about a fire. Like, I’ll be zipping up my tool bag, right? Or I'll be walking out to the truck after checking a panel or a disconnect for the third time, and I’m thinking, 'Okay, good job, time to head out.' 

But then my brain just goes, 'Hey, what if you missed one loose neutral?' And I mean, in my trade, a loose neutral is bad news. That’s how you get arcing, and arcing builds up heat, and next thing you know, you’ve got a fire inside a wall cavity where nobody can see it until the whole house is going up in the middle of the night. So I try to tell myself, 'No, you checked it, you tightened it, you saw the torque mark.' I try to just shake it off. I really do. I’ll turn the radio up in the truck, or I'll try to think about what I'm making for dinner, but the thought just... it just follows me. 

It follows me all the way home. It's like it sits there in the passenger seat with me, just nagging and nagging that I left something that could start a fire, and that I’m going to be responsible for burning some family's house down because I was too lazy to look one more time. And even when I know it doesn't make sense, because I've been doing this since I was twenty-something and I've never caused a fire, the thought just will not leave me alone. It just plays on a loop.

latest_inference.note: The patient's presentation of persistent, intrusive thoughts (e.g., fear of causing a fire due to a loose neutral) and repetitive behaviors (e.g., checking panels repeatedly, taking photos for reassurance) that are performed in response to the anxiety caused by these thoughts strongly aligns with Obsessive-Compulsive Disorder (OCD). Other candidates such as F43.22 (adjustment disorder with anxiety), F41.1 (generalized anxiety disorder), or depressive disorders (F32.1, F32.2, F33.1, F33.2) are less likely given the clear presence of obsessions and compulsions that are not better explained by another condition. No further questioning is needed as the clinical picture is consistent with F42.2.

Major depressive disorder (F32.1, F32.2, F33.1, F33.2) remains a consideration due to the potential secondary mood impact, though not yet endorsed in this initial report.
